title: Two-stage Miller OTA
description: The classic two-stage Miller operational transconductance amplifier: a differential input stage (input pair + current-mirror load) driving a common-source second stage, with a compensation capacitor $C_c$ bridging the second stage (Miller pole-splitting). $C_c$ is the compensation knob: it sets the dominant pole and hence the unity-gain bandwidth GBW = $g_{m1}/(2*\pi*C_c)$. The feedforward path through $C_c$ creates a right-half-plane zero $z = g_{m2}/C_c$ that erodes phase; the $R_z = 1/g_{m2}$ nulling resistor removes it. The phase-margin and second-pole equations are ESTIMATE-grade small-signal approximations for sizing intuition — the simulator owns stability sign-off. The first stage is drawn with both of its sides, because they do not sit at the same voltages. On the diode side the mirror device's drain is its own gate, one diode drop below the supply. On the output side the mirror's output device and the pair's output-side device share a drain that is the second stage's gate, so it sits one second-stage $V_{GS}$ below the supply instead. The stage is drawn at rest, as the feedback around the amplifier holds it: the output, and with it the second stage's gate, sits where the loop puts it, and the two inputs sit apart by whatever offset that takes. The currents are stated the way the circuit sets them: the bias reference is programmed with $I_1$, the tail device shares that reference's gate and width, the two input devices are one width and carry what the tail delivers between them, each its own share, and the second stage carries what its load delivers: the load is a second mirror output of the same reference, on its gate at $K_2$ times its width, so the stage-2 current is $K_2 I_1$ less that mirror's drain-voltage error, and the second-stage device is handed it. The mirror's output device is tied to its diode-side partner — the same width at the same gate-source voltage — and its current is read from the table at its own drain voltage. The share is solved, by a design constraint, so that the currents at the stage-1 output balance: the pair's output-side device takes exactly what the mirror's output device returns. Wherever the two levels differ, the two input devices then need different gate-source voltages for their currents, and the systematic-offset equation reports that difference directly. Entered from the COMMON MODE like the 5T: the input pair's tail node is solved by a second design constraint so the produced $CM_{in}$, the tail node plus the mean of the two gate-source voltages, equals $CM_{dc}$, fixing the pair's body bias and both drain-source voltages outright. Every bias gate is drawn — the tail device and the second-stage load on the bias reference's gate, the mirror's output device on its diode side's — so the only ports are the two input gates, which the application drives. On the demo NMOS table every device sizes against the same data, so the sign params stay at +1.

params.name: CL
params.note: output load capacitance

params.name: Av_target
params.note: two-stage DC gain target: 100 (40 dB), a 1 % static error in unity feedback, is a loose floor for a general-purpose two-stage amplifier, which commonly reaches 60 to 80 dB. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: GBW_target
params.note: unity-gain bandwidth target into the 5 pF load: a few megahertz is the range of a general-purpose two-stage amplifier biased at tens of microamps. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: PM_target
params.note: phase-margin target; the PM equation is estimate-grade

params.name: SR_target
params.note: slew-rate target: 5 V/us moves a 1 V step in 200 ns, in keeping with a few-megahertz general-purpose amplifier driving 5 pF. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: C1_est
params.note: stage-1 output node cap (stage-2 gate + drain parasitics + wiring); refine from the stage-2 device cgg plus extraction

params.name: CM_dc
params.note: the input common mode the application presents. The engine places the tail node so the sheet sits exactly here; sweep it to trace the common-mode axis. This sheet claims no operating range: stage 1 does not close on sky130-class supplies at these defaults, and range ends that cannot be met honestly would be theater — see the single-stage OTAs for the pattern.

params.name: V_tail
params.note: the input pair's tail node. Solved rather than set: searched between min and max (the range it is searched in, not slider bounds) until the produced common mode equals CM_dc. Fixes the pair's body bias and both of its drain-source voltages in one stroke, and it is the tail device's drain-source voltage, so it also sets the current the tail delivers. An end of the range where the relation does not evaluate is stepped inward silently, and the searched range is reported only if the search then fails. On a process whose PMOS diode eats most of the rail, the top of the range leaves the diode-side input device almost no drain-source voltage under the mirror diode drop; raising gm_id_ld1 (a smaller diode drop) is the knob that gives it room

params.name: Cc
params.note: Miller compensation cap: sets the dominant pole and GBW = gm1/(2*pi*Cc)

params.name: I1
params.note: the current the bias reference is programmed to — the one current on the sheet that is typed. The tail device mirrors it 1:1 and the second-stage load K2:1 through the shared gate, and each delivers it less its own drain-voltage error (the tail node normally sits below the reference's diode drop, the output above it); the slew limits, the bandwidth and the supply current are computed from what is delivered, not from this number

params.name: K2
params.note: mirror ratio of the second-stage load, as a width ratio: the load sits on the bias reference's gate at K2 times its width and at its length, so it is a mirror output of that reference and the device that sets the stage-2 current. It delivers K2 times I1 less its drain-voltage error — its drain is the output, above the reference's diode drop — and the second-stage device carries what it delivers. Raising it buys stage-2 slew and a higher second pole for supply current

params.name: out_share
params.note: the share of the tail current the pair's output-side device carries at rest — solved, not set. The stage-1 output is a high-impedance node, held where it is by the feedback around the amplifier, so in the resting circuit the current the pair's output-side device takes is exactly the current the mirror's output device returns: the engine searches for the share at which the two are equal, the current law at the stage-1 output. The diode-side device carries the rest, so the two add up to what the tail delivers by construction. The share is one half only where the second stage's gate-source voltage equals the mirror's diode drop. It is searched between 0.01 and 0.99, a share of the tail current that leaves each device some of it; the stored value is never read

params.name: gm_id_in
params.note: input-pair inversion, set on the output-side device; the diode-side device copies its width and carries the rest of the tail current

params.name: gm_id_ld1
params.note: stage-1 mirror-load inversion, set on the diode side and inherited by the output side through the shared gate

params.name: gm_id_tail
params.note: inversion level of the bias reference, which the tail device and the second-stage load inherit through the shared gate: a higher V* costs headroom at the tail node and output swing at the load

params.name: gm_id_s2
params.note: stage-2 device inversion

params.name: L_tail
params.note: length of the bias reference, the tail device and the second-stage load, which mirror at one length: longer shrinks each mirror's drain-voltage error and the load's output conductance

params.name: V_out2
params.note: stage-2 output DC level; sets both stage-2 devices' vds. The stage-2 device and its current-source load meet at a high-impedance output that nothing on this sheet holds; the feedback the application closes around the amplifier holds it here

params.name: out_sign
params.note: vds sign of the stage-2 device table (PMOS common source): +1 for the N-style demo axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis

params.name: ld1o_sign
params.note: vds sign of the table the stage-1 mirror's output device reads: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis. The diode side needs none — its drain follows its own gate in whichever convention its table uses. Read both sides of the mirror from the same table: the gate voltage they share is passed in that table's convention

params.name: vos_sys_target
params.note: systematic input offset budget. The offset is set by how far the second stage's gate-source voltage sits from the stage-1 mirror's diode drop, referred to the input through the first-stage gain, so this is the budget for leaving the two unequal: 50 mV between them at a first-stage gain of 50 is 1 mV

doc.title: Tail current source
doc.description: The tail device, on the bias reference's gate at the reference's width: a 1:1 mirror of the programmed current, with the tail node as its drain-source voltage. Its current is read off the table rather than typed — the reference sits at its own diode drop and this device at $V_{tail}$, so it delivers the programmed current scaled by what that difference in $V_{DS}$ does through its $g_{ds}$. It leaves saturation when $V_{tail}$ falls below its own $V_{dsat}$, which is what the tail-headroom equation watches.

params.name: Wx
params.note: the bias reference's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgsx
params.note: the bias reference's gate voltage — the gate wire the two share

params.name: vx
params.note: the tail node

doc.title: Stage-1 mirror-load device, diode side
doc.description: The diode-connected side of the stage-1 current-mirror load. It carries the current of the input device below it — what the tail delivers less the output-side device's share — and its drain is its gate, so it sits one $V_{GS}$ below the supply whatever the stage-1 output does. That gate is the mirror node: this device's width and gate voltage are what the output side copies.

doc.title: Stage-2 common-source device
doc.description: The second-stage gain device carrying the full stage-2 current — what its load delivers — at the output DC level. Its gm sets the RHP zero, the second pole, and the nulling resistor; its gate capacitance dominates the stage-1 output node cap.

params.name: vx
params.note: signed to this table's axis convention

doc.title: Stage-1 mirror-load device, output side
doc.description: The output side of the stage-1 mirror load, on the diode side's gate at the diode side's width. Its drain is the stage-1 output, and that node is the second stage's gate, so this device sits one second-stage $V_{GS}$ below the supply rather than one diode drop. Its current is read off the table at that drain voltage rather than typed: wherever the two levels differ it is not the diode side's current, and the difference is part of the systematic offset the sheet reports. Its output conductance loads the first-stage gain.

params.name: Wx
params.note: the diode side's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgsx
params.note: the diode side's gate voltage — the mirror node the two share, in the sign convention of the diode side's table

params.name: vx
params.note: the supply down to the stage-1 output, signed to this table's axis convention

doc.title: Stage-1 input-pair device, output side
doc.description: The input device whose drain is the stage-1 output — the second stage's gate — sized at its share of what the tail delivers. The pair's two devices share a gate drive and a source but not a drain, so the tail current does not split evenly between them, and this is the one whose output conductance loads the first-stage gain. Its source sits at the tail node — that is its body bias — and its drain-source voltage is what is left between the stage-1 output and that source. Its width is what its partner on the diode side copies; its gate-source voltage differs from its partner's by the input offset that holds the stage-1 output where it is.

params.name: vx
params.note: from the stage-1 output down to the tail node

params.name: vsbx
params.note: the tail node

doc.title: Stage-1 input-pair device, diode side
doc.description: The input device whose drain is the mirror node, in one branch with the diode-connected mirror device above it. It is the output-side device's width, carrying the rest of what the tail delivers: a matched pair is one width, so its width is copied, and its current is given, which makes this a width-and-current sizing — the table is inverted at that current density for the gate-source voltage it takes. Its source sits at the tail node like its partner's, but its drain sits one mirror diode drop below VDD instead of at the stage-1 output. Wherever the two drains or the two currents differ, its gate-source voltage differs from its partner's, and that difference is the input offset the sheet reports.

params.name: Wx
params.note: the output-side device's width — the pair is matched

params.name: Ix
params.note: what the tail delivers less the output-side device's share

params.name: vx
params.note: from the mirror node down to the tail node

params.name: vsbx
params.note: the tail node

equations.name: CM_in
equations.note: the input common mode this bias produces — an OUTPUT here, not a setting: the tail node plus the mean of the two input devices' gate-source voltages, the level the two inputs sit about. It rises monotonically with the tail node, so the design constraint that places the tail node from CM_dc is a well-posed one-unknown search

equations.name: V_mir
equations.note: the stage-1 mirror node — the diode side's drain and the gate the two mirror devices share, one diode drop below the supply

equations.name: V1
equations.note: stage-1 output DC. Derived, not typed: this node is the second stage's gate, so it sits one second-stage gate-source voltage below the supply (abs() keeps both table conventions working). It is the drain of the mirror's output device and of the pair's output-side device, and it is not the mirror node: the two levels differ by the difference between the second stage's gate-source voltage and the mirror's diode drop

equations.name: gm1
equations.note: stage-1 transconductance into the stage-1 output node. Each input device turns half the differential input into current: the diode-side half reaches the output through the mirror, whose current gain is its output device's $g_m$ over its diode device's, and the output-side half arrives directly. It is one input device's $g_m$ where the two sides sit at the same levels

equations.name: gm2
equations.note: stage-2 transconductance: sets the RHP zero, the second pole, and the nulling resistor

equations.name: GBW
equations.note: Miller-compensated unity-gain bandwidth (input gm into the compensation cap)

equations.name: wc
equations.note: angular unity-gain crossover (2*pi*GBW), the frequency the phase-margin estimate is read at

equations.name: z_rhp
equations.note: the right-half-plane zero the feedforward path through Cc would place, kept as a reference point for the UNCOMPENSATED stage: the Rz = 1/gm2 nulling resistor below moves it to infinity, which is why the phase-margin equation carries no zero term

equations.name: p2
equations.note: non-dominant (output) pole ESTIMATE; C1_est is the stage-1 output-node cap — refine it from the stage-2 cgg plus extraction

equations.name: Rz
equations.note: nulling resistor Rz = 1/gm2 that moves the RHP zero to infinity

equations.name: PM
equations.note: ESTIMATE: crossover phase lag from the second pole alone, because the Rz = 1/gm2 nulling resistor removes the RHP zero. The simulator owns stability sign-off

equations.name: SR
equations.note: the smaller slew limit: the current the tail device delivers charging Cc, or the current the second-stage load delivers charging CL

equations.name: Av1
equations.note: stage-1 gain into the two conductances on the stage-1 output node: the pair's output-side device and the mirror's output device, each read at that node's level

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance the amplifier presents at its output — stage two's own output conductance in parallel with its load device's. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this equation is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av2
equations.note: stage-2 common-source gain into its own and the load conductances

equations.name: Av
equations.note: two-stage DC gain (product of the stage gains)

equations.name: vos_sys
equations.note: input-referred systematic offset — the difference of the two input devices' gate-source voltages at rest, read directly: the input offset the feedback holding the output, and with it the second stage's gate, has to apply. The mirror's output device sits at the second stage's gate voltage instead of the mirror's diode drop, so it returns a different current than its diode side carries, and the pair's output-side device has to carry that current instead of an even share; its drain sits at that same level instead of at the mirror node, so even at equal currents the two input devices would need different gate-source voltages. It is zero when the second stage's gate-source voltage equals the mirror's diode drop — the classic condition that the second-stage device and the mirror devices run at one current density

equations.name: tail_headroom
equations.note: how far the tail node sits above the tail device's saturation voltage — exact here, because the tail node is the variable rather than something inferred from a common mode

equations.name: cgg2
equations.note: stage-2 gate capacitance — the dominant term in the stage-1 output cap C1_est; compare to refine the estimate

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance one input terminal presents — the gate capacitance of a single input device. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it, so a driving stage sees more than this. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the current the tail device delivers plus the current the second-stage load delivers. The reference branch that programs the tail and the load is shared bias infrastructure, typically one reference feeding several stages, and is not counted here. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: two-stage DC gain meets the target
the worse of the two slew limits meets the target
the compensated bandwidth (gm1/(2*pi*Cc)) meets the target
ESTIMATE-grade phase margin; the simulator owns the real stability sign-off

where the RHP zero would sit WITHOUT the nulling resistor: above crossover (equivalently gm2 >= gm1), or an uncompensated version of this stage loses its phase margin. With Rz = 1/gm2 in place the zero is gone and this is a design-margin reading, not a stability condition

checks.lhs: min(V_mir - V_tail - in__vdsat, V1 - V_tail - ino__vdsat)
checks.note: the pair's two drains sit at different levels — one a mirror diode drop below the supply, the other at the second stage's gate — so this watches whichever device has less room. Trips when the tail node is pushed so high that device runs out of drain-source voltage — lower gm/ID on the mirror or on the second stage spends less of the supply above it

the systematic input offset stays inside its budget. The stage-1 output sits at the second stage's gate, V1 = VDD - |vgs_s2|, while the mirror node sits at VDD - |vgs_ld1|, and the offset grows with the distance between the two — the classic W/L-ratio condition. Retune gm_id_s2 or gm_id_ld1 until the two gate-source voltages agree and the offset falls to zero
